claim: Adipogenesis in adulthood replaces fat cells that turn over and can contribute to the development of obesity.
source: Adipogenesis in adulthood replaces fat cells that turn over and can contribute to the development of obesity.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research (Faust et al., 1976; Faust et al., 1977; Hirsch and Han, 1969; Johnson and Hirsch, 1972) in the abstract.

claim: The proliferative potential of adipocyte progenitors in vivo is unknown.
source: However, the proliferative potential of adipocyte progenitors in vivo is unknown (Faust et al., 1976; Faust et al., 1977; Hirsch and Han, 1969; Johnson and Hirsch, 1972).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature indicating a gap in knowledge.

claim: Wild-type ES cells are the only source of mature adipocytes in chimeric animals derived from A-ZIP transgenic mice.
source: In the resulting chimeric animals, wild-type ES cells are the only source of mature adipocytes.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design and confirmed by immunohistochemistry data showing all adipocytes express YFP.

claim: Chimeric animals with low levels of chimerism showed significantly lower adipose tissue mass than animals with high levels of chimerism when fed a high-fat diet.
source: We found that when chimeric animals were fed a high-fat-diet, animals with low levels of chimerism showed a significantly lower adipose tissue mass than animals with high levels of chimerism.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: The difference in adipose tissue mass was attributed to variability in the amount of subcutaneous adipose tissue.
source: The difference in adipose tissue mass was attributed to variability in the amount of subcutaneous adipose tissue as the amount of visceral fat was independent of the level of chimerism.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing differential effects on subcutaneous versus visceral fat depots.

claim: The amount of visceral fat was independent of the level of chimerism.
source: The difference in adipose tissue mass was attributed to variability in the amount of subcutaneous adipose tissue as the amount of visceral fat was independent of the level of chimerism.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements showing no correlation between chimerism and visceral fat mass.

claim: Proliferative potential of adipocyte precursors is limited and can restrain the development of obesity.
source: Our findings thus suggest that proliferative potential of adipocyte precursors is limited and can restrain the development of obesity.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from the experimental data showing correlation between chimerism and adipose tissue mass.

claim: Obesity is associated with metabolic syndrome, which includes insulin resistance and diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension and an increased risk of cardiac disease.
source: Obesity is associated with a set of metabolic abnormalities, collectively known as the metabolic syndrome, which includes insulin resistance and diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension and an increased risk of cardiac disease (Grundy, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Lipodystrophy results from a reduced adipose tissue mass.
source: These same abnormalities also develop in lipodystrophy, a condition resulting from a reduced adipose tissue mass.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the definition of lipodystrophy.

claim: When the storage capacity of adipose tissue is exceeded, the result is 'lipid overflow', the deposition of excess lipid in peripheral tissues, leading to lipotoxicity, insulin resistance, and metabolic disease.
source: The fact that both increased and decreased adipose tissue mass can cause metabolic disease has suggested that when the storage capacity of adipose tissue is exceeded, the result is 'lipid overflow', the deposition of excess lipid in peripheral tissues, leading to lipotoxicity, insulin resistance, and metabolic disease (Huang-Doran et al., 2010).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The program controlling adipose tissue differentiation has been extensively studied in vitro.
source: While the program controlling adipose tissue differentiation has been extensively studied in vitro (Rosen and Spiegelman, 2000), less is known about the cellular mechanisms controlling adipose tissue formation in vivo or the factors that regulate its size (mass) (Rodeheffer et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Less is known about the cellular mechanisms controlling adipose tissue formation in vivo or the factors that regulate its size.
source: While the program controlling adipose tissue differentiation has been extensively studied in vitro (Rosen and Spiegelman, 2000), less is known about the cellular mechanisms controlling adipose tissue formation in vivo or the factors that regulate its size (mass) (Rodeheffer et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations indicating a gap in knowledge.

claim: Homeostasis of adipose tissue mass in adults is controlled by a negative feedback loop comprised of the hormone leptin and a set of neural targets that regulate food intake and metabolism.
source: In adults, homeostasis of adipose tissue mass is controlled by a negative feedback loop comprised of the hormone leptin and a set of neural targets that regulate food intake and metabolism (Friedman and Halaas, 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Surgical lipectomy leads to restoration of the removed fat presumably as a result of reduced levels of leptin.
source: Surgical lipectomy leads to restoration of the removed fat presumably as a result of reduced levels of leptin (Hernandez et al., 2011; Reyne et al., 1983; Knittle and Hirsch, 1968).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: Reduced leptin signaling leads to obesity in ob mice that lack leptin.
source: Reduced leptin signaling also leads to obesity in ob mice that lack leptin, and in animals fed a high fat diet (HFD) which causes leptin resistance (Friedman and Halaas, 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Animals fed a high fat diet develop leptin resistance.
source: Reduced leptin signaling also leads to obesity in ob mice that lack leptin, and in animals fed a high fat diet (HFD) which causes leptin resistance (Friedman and Halaas, 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In normal lean animals, the total number and size of adipocytes remains largely unchanged after adolescence.
source: In normal lean animals, the total number and size of adipocytes remains largely unchanged after adolescence (Knittle and Hirsch, 1968; Greenwood and Hirsch, 1974; Greenwood et al., 1979) with replacement of adipocytes that have turned over by newly formed adipocytes (Stiles et al., 1975; Hemmeryckx et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Adipocytes that have turned over are replaced by newly formed adipocytes.
source: In normal lean animals, the total number and size of adipocytes remains largely unchanged after adolescence (Knittle and Hirsch, 1968; Greenwood and Hirsch, 1974; Greenwood et al., 1979) with replacement of adipocytes that have turned over by newly formed adipocytes (Stiles et al., 1975; Hemmeryckx et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The development of obesity in adults on a high fat diet is a result of both adipocyte hypertrophy (increased cell size) and hyperplasia (the formation of new fat cells).
source: The development of obesity in adults on a high fat diet, is a result of both adipocyte hypertrophy, increased cell size, and hyperplasia, the formation of new fat cells (Spalding et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Homeostatic control of adipose tissue mass requires the coordinated regulation of adipocyte growth and proliferation.
source: Together, these observations suggest that homeostatic control of adipose tissue mass requires the coordinated regulation of adipocyte growth and proliferation.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited observations about adipocyte turnover and obesity development.

claim: Metabolic disease can develop when the capacity of adipose tissue to store lipid becomes limited, leading to its deposition in peripheral tissues.
source: The regulation of adipogenesis is thus of great importance because as mentioned, several lines of evidence have suggested that metabolic disease can develop when the capacity of adipose tissue to store lipid becomes limited, leading to its deposition in peripheral tissues (Huang-Doran et al., 2010; Unger, 2003; Medina-Gomez et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The mechanisms responsible for the increase in fat tissue in adults are not well understood.
source: However, the mechanisms responsible for the increase in fat tissue in adults are not well understood and the possibility that the proliferative potential of adipocyte precursors can be limited has not been directly studied.
evidence: This indicates a gap in current knowledge.

claim: The possibility that the proliferative potential of adipocyte precursors can be limited has not been directly studied.
source: However, the mechanisms responsible for the increase in fat tissue in adults are not well understood and the possibility that the proliferative potential of adipocyte precursors can be limited has not been directly studied.
evidence: This indicates a gap in current knowledge and justifies the study.

claim: A-ZIP transgenic mice have a genetic block in adipogenesis.
source: We addressed this by injecting labeled wild-type embryonic stem cells into blastocysts derived from lipodystrophic A-ZIP transgenic mice, which have a genetic block in adipogenesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the A-ZIP mouse model.

claim: The A-ZIP transgenic animals carry a dominant negative form of cEBPα leading to a block in adipogenesis resulting in severe congenital lipodystrophy.
source: The A-ZIP transgenic animals carry a dominant negative form of cEBPα leading to a block in adipogenesis resulting in severe congenital lipodystrophy (Moitra et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original characterization of the A-ZIP mouse model.

claim: All adipocytes in the chimeric animals are labeled by YFP.
source: We reasoned that because the WT ES-cells did not express the cEBPα transgene, the injected WT ES-cells should reconstitute the adipose tissue and that, if so, all adipocytes in the chimeric animals would be labeled by YFP.
evidence: This is confirmed by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: All of the adipocytes from WT:AZIP-chimeric mice expressed YFP.
source: All of the adipocytes from WT:AZIP-chimeric mice expressed YFP, assessed using IHC, confirming that the WT ES-cells were the only source of mature adipocytes (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Other tissues, including the adipose tissue stromal fraction, showed both YFP-positive and negative cells.
source: As expected, other tissues, including the adipose tissue stromal fraction, showed both YFP-positive and negative cells.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The extent of chimerism was quantified by calculating the ratio between the amount YFP-DNA and that of control genes, FABP4 or RPL23.
source: The extent of chimerism was quantified in a manner similar that used in a prior publication by calculating the ratio between the amount YFP-DNA (found only in cells derived from the injected WT ES-cells) and that of control genes, FABP4 or RPL23, which are similarly expressed in all cells (Stanger et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the methodology used, based on a prior publication.

claim: The extent of chimerism in blood cells was well correlated with the extent of chimerism in adipose tissue.
source: These animals are similarly chimeric in all tissues including adipose tissue and characterization of these animals confirmed that the extent of chimerism in blood cells was well correlated with the extent of chimerism in adipose tissue (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data (though not shown in the manuscript).

claim: The three groups of animals fed a chow diet showed similar growth curves between 4 weeks to 14 weeks.
source: The three groups of animals were fed a chow diet and showed similar growth curves between 4 weeks to 14 weeks (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Adipose tissue mass was reduced in the non-chimeric AZIP animals but was equivalent in WT:WT- and WT:AZIP-chimeras.
source: Adipose tissue mass was reduced in the non-chimeric AZIP animals but was equivalent in WT:WT- and WT:AZIP-chimeras; non-chimeric AZIP 9.5 ± 0.2%, WT:AZIP-chimeras 17.5 ± 1.6% and WT:WT-chimera 19.6 ± 1.6% (p=0.0002 for non-chimeric AZIP vs. WT:AZIP chimeras, see Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The levels of adipose tissue mass among the WT:AZIP chimeras was independent of the percent chimerism in chow-fed FVB animals.
source: The levels of adipose tissue mass among the WT:AZIP chimeras was independent of the percent chimerism and animals with either low or high levels of chimerism showed an equivalent adipose tissue mass. (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Serum leptin was not detectable in non-chimeric AZIPs.
source: Consistent with this, while serum leptin was not detectable in non-chimeric AZIPs, serum leptin in WT:AZIP-chimeras (8.5 ± 1.6 ng/mL) was equivalent to the level in WT:WT chimeras (12.1 ± 3.8 ng/mL; p=0.0002, and no significance respectively) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Serum leptin in WT:AZIP-chimeras was equivalent to the level in WT:WT chimeras in chow-fed FVB animals.
source: Consistent with this, while serum leptin was not detectable in non-chimeric AZIPs, serum leptin in WT:AZIP-chimeras (8.5 ± 1.6 ng/mL) was equivalent to the level in WT:WT chimeras (12.1 ± 3.8 ng/mL; p=0.0002, and no significance respectively) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1E.

claim: At 12 weeks, the hyperglycemia of AZIP(FVB) mice was completely normalized in WT:AZIP chimeras.
source: At 12 weeks, the hyperglycemia of AZIP(FVB) mice was completely normalized in WT:AZIP chimeras: 591.8 ± 8.2 mg/dL in non-chimeric AZIP animals (upper detection level of glucometer is 600 mg/dL) vs. 164.9 ± 6.7 mg/dl in the WT:AZIP-chimeric mice (p<0.0001; Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Liver triglyceride was normalized to WT levels in the WT:AZIP-chimeras.
source: Liver triglyceride (liver TG) was normalized to WT levels in the WT:AZIP-chimeras with a reduction from 731 ± 127 mmol/mg tissue in non-chimeric AZIP to 326 ± 69 mmol/mg tissue in WT:AZIP-chimeric animals (p=0.02; Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1H.

claim: WT:AZIP-chimeric animals had a plasma insulin level significantly lower than non-chimeric AZIP animals but still significantly higher than WT:WT-chimera.
source: WT:AZIP-chimeric animals had a plasma insulin level of 3.5 ± 1.0 ng/mL, vs. 9.3 ± 0.1 ng/mL for non-chimeric AZIP animals (p=0.005). However the insulin levels of the WT:AZIP-chimera was still significantly higher than WT:WT-chimera at 0.8 ± 0.04 ng/mL (p=0.05; Figure 1G), raising the possibility that subtle differences in the degree of chimerism could influence adiposity and that smaller levels of adiposity could lead to insulin resistance.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1G.

claim: ES-cells can reconstitute the adipose tissue mass in non-obese FVB AZIP animals on a chow diet.
source: These results show that ES-cells can reconstitute the adipose tissue mass in non-obese FVB AZIP animals on a chow diet and that the resulting adipocytes can function normally to suppress the metabolic abnormalities of lipodystrophy.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: The resulting adipocytes can function normally to suppress the metabolic abnormalities of lipodystrophy.
source: These results show that ES-cells can reconstitute the adipose tissue mass in non-obese FVB AZIP animals on a chow diet and that the resulting adipocytes can function normally to suppress the metabolic abnormalities of lipodystrophy.
evidence: This is inferred from the normalization of metabolic parameters shown in the data.

claim: In chow fed FVB derived chimeric mice, even a very limited amount of chimerism appears to be sufficient to restore normal adipose tissue mass.
source: These data also show that in chow fed FVB derived chimeric mice, even a very limited amount of chimerism appears to be sufficient to restore normal adipose tissue mass although the residual insulin resistance in the WT:AZIP-chimera indicated that this restoration may not be totally complete.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing no correlation between chimerism and adiposity in chow-fed FVB animals.

claim: The residual insulin resistance in the WT:AZIP-chimera indicated that restoration of adipose tissue may not be totally complete.
source: These data also show that in chow fed FVB derived chimeric mice, even a very limited amount of chimerism appears to be sufficient to restore normal adipose tissue mass although the residual insulin resistance in the WT:AZIP-chimera indicated that this restoration may not be totally complete.
evidence: This is inferred from the elevated insulin levels in WT:AZIP chimeras compared to WT:WT chimeras.

claim: C57BL/6J is the strain that is most prone to develop obesity on a high fat diet.
source: However, since C57BL/6J is the strain that is most prone to develop obesity on a high fat diet (HFD) (Montgomery et al., 2013), we transferred the A-ZIP transgene to the C57BL/6J strain by backcrossing the transgene for six or more generations.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Genetic background can have a significant impact on the phenotype of lipodystrophic A-ZIP transgenic mice.
source: Genetic background can have a significant impact on the phenotype of lipodystrophic A-ZIP transgenic mice.
evidence: This is established knowledge and is demonstrated by the differences between FVB and B6 AZIP mice described in the manuscript.

claim: On the FVB background, lipodystrophic animals develop severe metabolic abnormalities, including hyperglycemia, hyperinsulinemic, hyperlipidemia, and liver steatosis.
source: On the FVB background, lipodystrophic animals develop severe metabolic abnormalities, including hyperglycemia, hyperinsulinemic, hyperlipidemia, and liver steatosis (Moitra et al., 1998) (also see above).
evidence: This is supported by citation and by data presented earlier in the manuscript.

claim: C57BL/6J A-ZIP mice show reduced adipose tissue mass, low leptin levels and very prominent hepatic steatosis with only mild insulin resistance and normoglycemia.
source: In contrast, C57BL/6J A-ZIP (lipodystrophic) mice have been previously reported to show reduced adipose tissue mass, low leptin levels and very prominent hepatic steatosis with only mild insulin resistance and normoglycemia (Haluzik et al., 2004; Colombo et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The C57BL/6J AZIP animals showed reduced fat mass, mild insulin resistance, euglycemia, and hepatic steatosis.
source: Consistent with previous reports, the C57BL/6J AZIP animals we generated showed reduced fat mass, mild insulin resistance, euglycemia, and hepatic steatosis (see below).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: At three weeks of age, non-chimeric B6 AZIP-transgenic mice showed a reduced body weight compared to the chimeric WT:AZIP and WT:WT animals.
source: At three weeks of age, non-chimeric B6 AZIP-transgenic mice showed a reduced body weight compared to the chimeric WT:AZIP and WT:WT animals (p<0.01) but this difference diminished in older animals (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There was a small but significant difference in fat mass and serum leptin among the three groups with the WT:AZIP animals intermediate between the other two.
source: There was also a small but significant difference in fat mass (when corrected for the very enlarged fatty liver of the AZIP mice) and serum leptin among the three groups with the WT:AZIP animals intermediate between the other two (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: Despite their slightly lower adiposity relative to the WT:WT chimeras, there was no effect of the level of chimerism on adiposity or serum leptin in the WT:AZIP chimeras on chow diet.
source: However, despite their slightly lower adiposity relative to the WT:WT chimeras, there was no effect of the level of chimerism on adiposity or serum leptin in the WT:AZIP chimeras. (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: C57Bl/6J WT:AZIP animals with low levels of chimerism showed similar levels of adiposity and serum leptin to those with high levels of chimerism on chow diet.
source: Thus, similar to FVB animals on a chow diet, C57Bl/6J WT:AZIP animals with low levels of chimerism showed similar levels of adiposity and serum leptin to those with high levels of chimerism (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: The correlation between serum leptin and adiposity was the same in WT:AZIP and WT:WT chimeras.
source: The correlation between serum leptin and adiposity was the same in WT:AZIP and WT:WT chimeras suggesting that leptin production by adipocytes was similar in WT:AZIP adipose tissue.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing similar slopes in the leptin-adiposity relationship.

claim: Leptin production by adipocytes was similar in WT:AZIP adipose tissue compared to WT:WT.
source: The correlation between serum leptin and adiposity was the same in WT:AZIP and WT:WT chimeras suggesting that leptin production by adipocytes was similar in WT:AZIP adipose tissue.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar correlation between leptin and adiposity in both groups.

claim: Histologic analysis of the adipose tissue of WT:AZIP- and WT:WT-chimeras with comparable levels of chimerism showed similar fat cell sizes.
source: Consistent with this, histologic analysis of the adipose tissue of WT:AZIP- and WT:WT-chimeras with comparable levels of chimerism showed similar fat cell sizes suggesting the decrease in adiposity in the WT:AZIP chimeric animals was a result of a decreased cell number (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The decrease in adiposity in the WT:AZIP chimeric animals was a result of a decreased cell number.
source: Consistent with this, histologic analysis of the adipose tissue of WT:AZIP- and WT:WT-chimeras with comparable levels of chimerism showed similar fat cell sizes suggesting the decrease in adiposity in the WT:AZIP chimeric animals was a result of a decreased cell number (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of similar cell sizes but different adiposity levels.

claim: Plasma glucose was significantly reduced in WT:AZIP and WT:WT chimeras, compared to non-chimeric AZIPs in chow-fed B6 animals.
source: Plasma glucose was significantly reduced in WT:AZIP and WT:WT chimeras, compared to non-chimeric AZIPs (Figure 2E) but the reduction of glucose did not correlate with the level of chimerism (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The reduction of glucose did not correlate with the level of chimerism in chow-fed B6 animals.
source: Plasma glucose was significantly reduced in WT:AZIP and WT:WT chimeras, compared to non-chimeric AZIPs (Figure 2E) but the reduction of glucose did not correlate with the level of chimerism (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: C57BL/6J AZIP mice are hyperinsulinemic.
source: C57BL/6J AZIP mice are hyperinsulinemic and the WT:AZIP-chimeras had significantly lower plasma insulin levels compared to non-chimeric AZIP with reduced insulin levels that were equivalent to those of WT:WT-chimeras; controls (117 ± 10 ng/mL in AZIPS vs. 8.2 ± 3.6 ng/mL in WT:AZIPs, p<0.0001; Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The WT:AZIP-chimeras had significantly lower plasma insulin levels compared to non-chimeric AZIP with reduced insulin levels that were equivalent to those of WT:WT-chimeras in chow-fed B6 animals.
source: C57BL/6J AZIP mice are hyperinsulinemic and the WT:AZIP-chimeras had significantly lower plasma insulin levels compared to non-chimeric AZIP with reduced insulin levels that were equivalent to those of WT:WT-chimeras; controls (117 ± 10 ng/mL in AZIPS vs. 8.2 ± 3.6 ng/mL in WT:AZIPs, p<0.0001; Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2F.

claim: At 24 weeks, the enlarged liver of C57Bl/6J AZIPs was fully normalized in the WT:AZIP-chimeras.
source: Similarly, at 24 weeks, the enlarged liver associated of C57Bl/6J AZIPs was fully normalized in the WT:AZIP-chimeras and the liver size was indistinguishable from the size in the WT:WT-chimeras (5.8 ± 0.5 for AZIPs vs 2.1 ± 0.2 g in WT:AZIPs; p=6xE-4 and 1.7 ± 0.1 g for WT:WTs; Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2G.

claim: There was no significant correlation between the level of chimerism and liver weight in chow-fed B6 animals.
source: Here again there was no significant correlation between the level of chimerism and liver weight (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Even low amounts of chimerism can correct the features of the metabolic syndrome of B6 AZIP animals on a chow diet.
source: In aggregate, these data show that even low amounts of chimerism can correct the features of the metabolic syndrome of B6 AZIP animals on a chow diet.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing normalization of metabolic parameters.

claim: The adiposity and plasma leptin concentration of the WT:AZIP chimeras was slightly lower than in the WT:WTs chimeras on chow diet.
source: However, similar to the FVB chimera, the adiposity and plasma leptin concentration of the WT:AZIP chimeras was slightly lower than in the WT:WTs chimeras raising the possibility that low chimerism, potentially indicating a lower number of adipocyte progenitors, may be constraining the ultimate size of the adipose tissue mass.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data comparing WT:AZIP and WT:WT chimeras.

claim: Low chimerism, potentially indicating a lower number of adipocyte progenitors, may be constraining the ultimate size of the adipose tissue mass.
source: However, similar to the FVB chimera, the adiposity and plasma leptin concentration of the WT:AZIP chimeras was slightly lower than in the WT:WTs chimeras raising the possibility that low chimerism, potentially indicating a lower number of adipocyte progenitors, may be constraining the ultimate size of the adipose tissue mass.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed differences in adiposity.

claim: As early as week 11 (after five weeks of HFD), WT:AZIP-chimeras as a group had significantly lower weights relative to the WT:WT-chimeras and significantly higher weights than the non-chimeric AZIPs.
source: We found greater variability of weight among the animals on a HFD compared to those on a chow diet, and as early as week 11 (after five weeks of HFD) we found that the WT:AZIP-chimeras as a group had significantly lower weights relative to the WT:WT-chimeras and significantly higher weights than the non-chimeric AZIPs.
evidence: This is supported by the growth curve data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: At 24 weeks old (after 18 weeks of HFD), WT:WT chimeras weighed an average of 56.6 ± 1 grams while non-chimeric AZIP animals only weighed an average of 38.1 ± 0.8 grams.
source: At the conclusion of the study (24 weeks old and after 18 weeks of HFD), WT:WT chimeras weighed an average of 56.6 ± 1 grams while non-chimeric AZIP animals only weighed an average of 38.1 ± 0.8 grams.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements.

claim: WT:AZIPs with very low chimerism (1–10%) weighed 36.3 ± 0.6 grams at 24 weeks.
source: WT:AZIPs with very low chimerism (1–10%) weighed 36.3 ± 0.6 grams, WT:AZIPs with medium chimerism (10–30%) weighed an average of 40.6 ± 1.2 grams and WT:AZIPs with high chimerism (>30%) weighed 44.6 ± 1.8 grams (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: WT:AZIPs with medium chimerism (10–30%) weighed an average of 40.6 ± 1.2 grams at 24 weeks.
source: WT:AZIPs with very low chimerism (1–10%) weighed 36.3 ± 0.6 grams, WT:AZIPs with medium chimerism (10–30%) weighed an average of 40.6 ± 1.2 grams and WT:AZIPs with high chimerism (>30%) weighed 44.6 ± 1.8 grams (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: WT:AZIPs with high chimerism (>30%) weighed 44.6 ± 1.8 grams at 24 weeks.
source: WT:AZIPs with very low chimerism (1–10%) weighed 36.3 ± 0.6 grams, WT:AZIPs with medium chimerism (10–30%) weighed an average of 40.6 ± 1.2 grams and WT:AZIPs with high chimerism (>30%) weighed 44.6 ± 1.8 grams (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Weight-gain correlated with the degree of chimerism in WT:AZIP animals on HFD.
source: When the level of adiposity was analyzed relative to percent chimerism, a clear pattern emerged in which weight-gain correlated with the degree of chimerism with WT:AZIP animals with the highest percentage chimerism gaining significantly more weight than chimeras with a lower level of chimerism (Figure 3B; linear regression of WT: AZIPs is Y = 0.1876*X+36.00, R^2 = 0.4721).
evidence: This is supported by data and linear regression analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Weight gain among WT:WT chimera was independent of chimerism.
source: As expected, weight gain among WT: WT chimera was independent of chimerism (Figure 3B; WT:WT linear regression is Y = −0.04248*X+57.26, R^2 = 0.02877).
evidence: This is supported by data and linear regression analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: On a HFD, the percent fat of WT:AZIPs was intermediate between that of non-chimeric AZIPs and WT:WT-chimera and correlated with the extent of chimerism.
source: On a HFD, the percent fat of WT:AZIPs, assessed using MRI, was intermediate between that of non-chimeric AZIPs and WT:WT-chimera and, as was the case for weight, correlated with the extent of chimerism. (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by MRI data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: WT:AZIP-chimeras were markedly less obese compared to WT:WT chimeric animals on HFD.
source: Consistent with the previous studies of the chow fed animals, WT:AZIP-chimeras were markedly less obese compared to WT:WT chimeric animals.
evidence: This is supported by the adiposity measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: The increase in fat percentage correlated linearly with an increase in chimerism in WT:AZIP animals on HFD.
source: The increase in fat percentage correlated linearly with an increase in chimerism such that at the highest levels of chimerism, adiposity approached that of the WT:WT chimeric animals (Figure 3C; Y = 0.3128*X + 13.28, R^2 = 0.5633 for WT:AZIPS on HFD and Y = 0.01217*X + 42.40, R^2 = 0.003468 for WT:WTs on HFD).
evidence: This is supported by data and linear regression analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: At the highest levels of chimerism, adiposity approached that of the WT:WT chimeric animals on HFD.
source: The increase in fat percentage correlated linearly with an increase in chimerism such that at the highest levels of chimerism, adiposity approached that of the WT:WT chimeric animals (Figure 3C; Y = 0.3128*X + 13.28, R^2 = 0.5633 for WT:AZIPS on HFD and Y = 0.01217*X + 42.40, R^2 = 0.003468 for WT:WTs on HFD).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Non-chimeric AZIPs showed approximately 10% body fat, which was fully accounted for by the enlarged, steatotic liver.
source: While the non-chimeric AZIPs did show approximately 10% body fat, as mentioned, this low level of adiposity was fully accounted for by the enlarged, steatotic liver in these animals.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that removing the liver reduced body fat to 1.2%.

claim: When the liver was removed post-mortem, the body fat percentage of non-chimeric AZIPs fell to 1.2% ± 0.1.
source: Thus, when the liver was removed post-mortem, the body fat percentage of non-chimeric AZIPs fell to 1.2% ± 0.1 (Data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements (though data not shown).

claim: The serum leptin of WT:AZIPs was intermediate between that of AZIPs and WT:WTs on HFD.
source: Consistent with the measures of adiposity, the serum leptin of WT:AZIPs was also intermediate between that of AZIPs and WT:WTs and, similar to adiposity, leptin levels increased linearly with increasing chimerism in WT:AZIPs (Figure 3D; linear regression of WT:AZIPs Y = 0.6495*X-0.1076, R^2 = 0.09426).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Leptin levels increased linearly with increasing chimerism in WT:AZIPs on HFD.
source: Consistent with the measures of adiposity, the serum leptin of WT:AZIPs was also intermediate between that of AZIPs and WT:WTs and, similar to adiposity, leptin levels increased linearly with increasing chimerism in WT:AZIPs (Figure 3D; linear regression of WT:AZIPs Y = 0.6495*X-0.1076, R^2 = 0.09426).
evidence: This is supported by data and linear regression analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Leptin levels were unaffected by the extent of chimerism in WT:WT chimera on HFD.
source: Leptin levels were unaffected by the extent of chimerism in WT:WT chimera (Y = 0.2372*X+112.7, R^2 = 0.05183) while the non-chimeric AZIP animals had undetectable plasma leptin levels.
evidence: This is supported by data and linear regression analysis.

claim: Non-chimeric AZIP animals had undetectable plasma leptin levels on HFD.
source: Leptin levels were unaffected by the extent of chimerism in WT:WT chimera (Y = 0.2372*X+112.7, R^2 = 0.05183) while the non-chimeric AZIP animals had undetectable plasma leptin levels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements.

claim: When WT:AZIP-chimeras are placed on a high fat diet, lower levels of chimerism limits weight gain and adiposity.
source: These data show that when WT:AZIP-chimeras are placed on a high fat diet, lower levels of chimerism limits weight gain and adiposity, as well as the amount of leptin that circulates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing correlation between chimerism and adiposity on HFD.

claim: The WT:AZIP-chimera with ~80% chimerism, or above, became markedly obese with weights that approached that of wild-type animals.
source: Importantly, the WT:AZIP-chimera with ~80% chimerism, or above, became markedly obese with weights that approached that of wild-type animals.
evidence: This is supported by the weight data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The injected ES cells were capable of reconstituting the adipose tissue mass but only when the level of chimerism is high.
source: This indicates that the injected ES cells were capable of reconstituting the adipose tissue mass but only when the level of chimerism is high (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that high chimerism animals reached wild-type adiposity levels.

claim: A subset of hyperinsulinemic patients have reduced adipose tissue mass.
source: Recent studies have indicated that a subset of hyperinsulinemic patients have reduced adipose tissue mass, suggesting the possibility that a reduced storage capacity of the adipose depot can have metabolic consequences (Scott et al., 2014; Yaghootkar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: A reduced storage capacity of the adipose depot can have metabolic consequences.
source: Recent studies have indicated that a subset of hyperinsulinemic patients have reduced adipose tissue mass, suggesting the possibility that a reduced storage capacity of the adipose depot can have metabolic consequences (Scott et al., 2014; Yaghootkar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Non-chimeric AZIPs displayed severe metabolic consequences including hyperglycemia, hyperinsulinemia and hepatomegaly on HFD.
source: We found that, as expected, non-chimeric AZIPs (chimerism below one percent) displayed severe metabolic consequences including hyperglycemia, hyperinsulinemia and hepatomegaly (Figure 3E, F and G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B, C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in the figures.

claim: All chimeric HFD WT:AZIP animals, regardless of degree of chimerism, showed similar levels of ad libitum glucose, fasting glucose, fasting insulin levels and liver mass relative to the WT:WT chimeras.
source: However, despite the fact that there was a reduced level of adiposity, all chimeric HFD WT:AZIP animals, regardless of degree of chimerism, showed similar levels of ad libitum glucose, fasting glucose, fasting insulin levels and liver mass relative to the WT:WT chimeras (Figure 3D, E and F, Figure 3—figure supplemnet 1D and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in the figures.

claim: Restoring even a very small level of adipose tissue in chimeric animals was capable of normalizing glucose and insulin to the levels seen in the WT:WT chimeras.
source: Thus restoring even a very small level of adipose tissue in chimeric animals was capable of normalizing glucose and insulin to the levels seen in the WT:WT chimeras.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing normalization of metabolic parameters.

claim: With levels of chimerism even as low as one percent, liver mass decreased from an average of 9.7 ± 0.5 to 3.1 ± 0.6 grams in WT:AZIPs.
source: With levels of chimerism even as low as one percent, liver mass decreased from an average of 9.7 ± 0.5 to 3.1 ± 0.6 grams in WT:AZIPs with all WT:WT chimeras averaging 3.2 ± 0.2 grams of liver (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3G.

claim: All animals showed similar levels of lean body mass on HFD.
source: All animals showed similar levels of lean body mass (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: WT:AZIPs with both high and low levels of chimerism all displayed the same levels of blood triglycerides and ketone bodies as wild-type chimeras on HFD.
source: Consistent with the above, WT:AZIPs with both high and low levels of chimerism all displayed the same levels of blood triglycerides and ketone bodies as wild-type chimeras (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G, H, I and J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in the figures.

claim: Animals with low levels of chimerism showed increased leptin levels relative to non-chimeric animals.
source: Animals with low levels of chimerism also showed increased leptin levels relative to non-chimeric animals raising the possibility that even a small increase of leptin levels could improve and often normalize the metabolic phenotype of this subgroup (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Even a small increase of leptin levels could improve and often normalize the metabolic phenotype.
source: Animals with low levels of chimerism also showed increased leptin levels relative to non-chimeric animals raising the possibility that even a small increase of leptin levels could improve and often normalize the metabolic phenotype of this subgroup (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: All WT:WT animals showed a similar weight of fat pads independent of the degree of chimerism.
source: All WT:WT animals showed a similar weight of fat pads independent of the degree of chimerism.
evidence: This is supported by the fat pad weight data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SubQ fat pad mass correlated positively and linearly with percent chimerism in WT:AZIP animals on HFD.
source: SubQ fat pad mass correlated positively and linearly with percent chimerism and SubQ fat in the animals with the highest chimerism approached that of the SubQ fat mass in WT:WT animals (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by data and linear regression analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: SubQ fat in the animals with the highest chimerism approached that of the SubQ fat mass in WT:WT animals.
source: SubQ fat pad mass correlated positively and linearly with percent chimerism and SubQ fat in the animals with the highest chimerism approached that of the SubQ fat mass in WT:WT animals (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There was no correlation between chimerism and the size of the visceral fat pads.
source: In contrast, there was no correlation between chimerism and the size of the visceral fat pads.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Visceral fat pads weighed a similar amount at all levels of chimerism, even at levels as low as one percent.
source: Visceral fat pads weighed a similar amount at all levels of chimerism, even at levels as low as one percent (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: All WT:AZIP chimeras had somewhat lower visceral fat pad mass than in WT:WT chimeras.
source: All WT:AZIP chimeras had somewhat lower visceral fat pad mass than in WT:WT chimeras.
evidence: This is supported by the visceral fat pad weight data.

claim: The subcutaneous and visceral depots are regulated differently.
source: These results show that the subcutaneous and visceral depots are regulated differently and that degree of chimerism only affects the size of subcutaneous depot.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential effects of chimerism on the two depot types.

claim: Degree of chimerism only affects the size of subcutaneous depot.
source: These results show that the subcutaneous and visceral depots are regulated differently and that degree of chimerism only affects the size of subcutaneous depot.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: There was no significant difference between fat cell size in either type of fat nor was there any correlation between size and the degree of chimerism.
source: There was no significant difference between fat cell size in either type of fat nor was there any correlation between size and the degree of chimerism (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by adipocyte size measurements shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The number of adipocytes per SubQ fat pad in WT:AZIP chimeras significantly increased with increasing percent chimerism.
source: Following from this, the number of adipocytes per SubQ fat pad in WT:AZIP chimeras significantly increased with increasing percent chimerism (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The average number of cells making up the WT:AZIP SubQ fat pad was 1.2 ± 0.2 E6 versus 2.6 ± 0.5 E6 in a WT:WT SubQ fat pad.
source: The average number of cells making up the WT:AZIP SubQ fat pad was 1.2 ± 0.2 E6 versus 2.6 ± 0.5 E6 in a WT:WT SubQ fat pad.
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data.

claim: In visceral fat depots, the number of adipocytes in the depots was unaffected by degree of chimerism.
source: Conversely, in visceral fat depots, the number of adipocytes in the depots was unaffected by degree of chimerism.
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: For visceral fat pads, there was an average number of 0.77 ± 0.6 E6 cells in WT:AZIPs and 1.7 ± 0.2 E6 cells in WT:WTs.
source: For visceral fat pads, there was an average number of 0.77 ± 0.6 E6 cells in WT:AZIPs and 1.7 ± 0.2 E6 cells in WT:WTs.
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data.

claim: There are reduced numbers of adipocytes in the subcutaneous depots of animals with low degrees of chimerism.
source: These data indicated that there are reduced numbers of adipocytes in the subcutaneous depots of animals with low degrees of chimerism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cell counting data.

claim: The differences in adiposity among chimeric animals resulted from differences in adipocyte number and not cell size.
source: Thus the differences in adiposity among chimeric animals resulted from differences in adipocyte number and not cell size, and there was a difference in adipocyte number in SubQ but not visceral fat.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cell size and cell number data.

claim: There was a difference in adipocyte number in SubQ but not visceral fat.
source: Thus the differences in adiposity among chimeric animals resulted from differences in adipocyte number and not cell size, and there was a difference in adipocyte number in SubQ but not visceral fat.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cell counting data.

claim: C57Bl/6J WT:AZIP-chimera fed a high fat diet with lower levels of chimerism developed a reduced adipose tissue mass compared to animals with a higher level of chimerism.
source: We found that C57Bl/6J WT:AZIP-chimera fed a high fat diet with lower levels of chimerism developed a reduced adipose tissue mass compared to animals with a higher level of chimerism.
evidence: This is the main finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Differences in the size of the subcutaneous depots in animals with lower levels of chimerism were fully accounted for by changes in cell number.
source: We also found that differences in the size of the subcutaneous depots in animals with lower levels of chimerism were fully accounted for by changes in cell number and that the percent chimerism did not affect adipocyte size in either visceral or subcutaneous fat pads.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cell size and cell number data.

claim: The percent chimerism did not affect adipocyte size in either visceral or subcutaneous fat pads.
source: We also found that differences in the size of the subcutaneous depots in animals with lower levels of chimerism were fully accounted for by changes in cell number and that the percent chimerism did not affect adipocyte size in either visceral or subcutaneous fat pads.
evidence: This is supported by adipocyte size measurements.

claim: Diet (chow versus HFD) did affect cell size as adipocytes from animals on a chow diet were on average smaller than adipocytes from animals on a high fat diet.
source: In contrast, diet (chow versus HFD) did affect cell size as adipocytes from animals on a chow diet were on average smaller than adipocytes from animals on a high fat diet.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing cell size data between chow and HFD animals.

claim: The level of chimerism is likely to reflect the number of progenitors.
source: The fact that the level of chimerism was correlated with cell number in the subcutaneous adipose depots is consistent with the possibility that the level of chimerism reflects the number of progenitors.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between chimerism and cell number.

claim: A reduced number of fat cell progenitors can limit the development of obesity.
source: Thus, these results suggest that a reduced number of fat cell progenitors can limit the development of obesity.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from the experimental data.

claim: Suitable markers specific for adipocyte progenitors in vivo are not yet available.
source: While studies directly assessing the number of progenitors would be necessary to further confirm this, suitable markers specific for adipocyte progenitors in vivo are not yet available.
evidence: This indicates a limitation in current methodology.

claim: Some studies have shown continued renewal of adipocytes in humans as well as new fat cell formation in rodents as obesity develops.
source: Thus while some studies have shown continued renewal of adipocytes in humans as well as new fat cell formation in rodents as obesity develops, other studies have suggested that there is a limited number of fat progenitors as animals enter maturity (Spalding et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2013; Rivera-Gonzalez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Other studies have suggested that there is a limited number of fat progenitors as animals enter maturity.
source: Thus while some studies have shown continued renewal of adipocytes in humans as well as new fat cell formation in rodents as obesity develops, other studies have suggested that there is a limited number of fat progenitors as animals enter maturity (Spalding et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2013; Rivera-Gonzalez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In a previous study on pancreas and liver development, the size of the pancreas was lower in animals with lower levels of chimerism.
source: In a previous study on pancreas and liver development, the same approach revealed that while the size of the pancreas was lower in animals with lower levels of chimerism, the size of liver was not (Stanger et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In a previous study on pancreas and liver development, the size of liver was not affected by chimerism.
source: In a previous study on pancreas and liver development, the same approach revealed that while the size of the pancreas was lower in animals with lower levels of chimerism, the size of liver was not (Stanger et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Liver possess considerable plasticity in size in response to various extrinsic signals such as after a partial hepatectomy.
source: This result correlated well with the fact that liver possess considerable plasticity in size in response to various extrinsic signals such as after a partial hepatectomy (Kang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Adipose tissue was more similar to the pancreas rather than liver with respect to the effect of chimerism on organ size.
source: We were surprised to find that adipose tissue was more similar to the pancreas rather than liver.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the results to prior studies.

claim: Subcutaneous and visceral fat also have different embryonic origins.
source: Subcutaneous and visceral fat also have different embryonic origins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about adipose tissue development.

claim: Subcutaneous inguinal white adipose tissue arises from the lateral mesoderm germ layer.
source: Subcutaneous inguinal white adipose tissue arises from the lateral mesoderm germ layer, as do blood cells which were used in this study to determine degree of chimerism.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Blood cells arise from the lateral mesoderm germ layer.
source: Subcutaneous inguinal white adipose tissue arises from the lateral mesoderm germ layer, as do blood cells which were used in this study to determine degree of chimerism.
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: Perigonadal white adipose tissue has a more heterogeneous origin from within the mesoderm germ layer with contributions from both paraxial and lateral mesoderm.
source: Perigonadal white adipose tissue has a more heterogeneous origin from within the mesoderm germ layer with contributions from both paraxial and lateral mesoderm (Luong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The level of chimerism in blood cells accurately reflects chimerism in subcutaneous adipose tissue.
source: Because blood cells and subcutaneous adipose tissue share a similar embryonic origin in the lateral mesoderm, we consider it likely the level of chimerism in blood cells accurately reflects chimerism in subcutaneous adipose tissue.
evidence: This is inferred from the shared embryonic origin.

claim: Chimerism in blood may not accurately reflect the extent of chimerism among the visceral fat precursors.
source: This is less certain for gonadal visceral fat which derives from all parts of the mesoderm germ layer. We did not observe a difference in the size of visceral adipose depots amongst our chimeric animals suggesting that either visceral fat is not dependent on progenitor number or alternatively that chimerism in blood did not accurately reflect the extent of chimerism among the visceral fat precursors.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Either visceral fat is not dependent on progenitor number or chimerism in blood did not accurately reflect the extent of chimerism among the visceral fat precursors.
source: We did not observe a difference in the size of visceral adipose depots amongst our chimeric animals suggesting that either visceral fat is not dependent on progenitor number or alternatively that chimerism in blood did not accurately reflect the extent of chimerism among the visceral fat precursors.
evidence: This presents two alternative interpretations of the data.

claim: The increased adiposity in mice was the result of increased amounts of subcutaneous, not visceral fat.
source: However, the increased adiposity in mice we observed was the result of increased amounts of subcutaneous, not visceral fat and thus this possibility would not alter our central conclusion.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing differential effects on the two depot types.

claim: The data are consistent with the possibility that the number of adipocyte progenitors constituting subcutaneous adipose tissue can be limiting for adiposity when animals are placed on a HFD.
source: The data are consistent with the possibility that the number of adipocyte progenitors constituting subcutaneous adipose tissue can be limiting for adiposity when animals are placed on a HFD.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from the experimental data.

claim: The size and cell number of subcutaneous adipose depots are dependent on the level of chimerism while visceral adipocytes are not.
source: We also found that the size and cell number of subcutaneous adipose depots are dependent on the level of chimerism while visceral adipocytes are not.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Restoration of only a very limited amount of adipose tissue can markedly improve the metabolic defects of lipodystrophic mice.
source: Finally, our data show that restoration of only a very limited amount of adipose tissue can markedly improve the metabolic defects of lipodystrophic mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing normalization of metabolic parameters.

claim: The development of metabolic abnormalities in lipodystrophic animals may to a large extent be a result of decreased leptin production.
source: Together with previous reports, this suggests that the development of metabolic abnormalities in lipodystrophic animals may to a large extent be a result of decreased leptin production (Rodeheffer et al., 2008; Gavrilova et al., 2000; Colombo et al., 2002) though it is possible that other adipocyte factors or metabolic functions of adipose tissue also contribute.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the data and supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Other adipocyte factors or metabolic functions of adipose tissue may also contribute to metabolic abnormalities in lipodystrophy.
source: Together with previous reports, this suggests that the development of metabolic abnormalities in lipodystrophic animals may to a large extent be a result of decreased leptin production (Rodeheffer et al., 2008; Gavrilova et al., 2000; Colombo et al., 2002) though it is possible that other adipocyte factors or metabolic functions of adipose tissue also contribute.
evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging other possible mechanisms.

claim: Subcutaneous fat stores have been associated with improved metabolic function in humans.
source: In humans, subcutaneous fat stores have been associated with improved metabolic function, whereas visceral fat accumulation correlates with metabolic dysfunction (Chusyd et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Visceral fat accumulation correlates with metabolic dysfunction in humans.
source: In humans, subcutaneous fat stores have been associated with improved metabolic function, whereas visceral fat accumulation correlates with metabolic dysfunction (Chusyd et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Subcutaneous and visceral fat stores show differences in innervation by the sympathetic nervous system.
source: Subcutaneous and visceral fat stores also show differences in innervation by the sympathetic nervous system and respond differently to leptin treatment (Wang et al., 2020; Chi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Subcutaneous and visceral fat stores respond differently to leptin treatment.
source: Subcutaneous and visceral fat stores also show differences in innervation by the sympathetic nervous system and respond differently to leptin treatment (Wang et al., 2020; Chi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There are multiple reports of differences in the response of subcutaneous and visceral depots as adiposity develops or after surgical fat removal.
source: Finally, there are multiple reports of differences in the response of these depots as adiposity develops or after surgical fat removal (Faust et al., 1977; Johnson and Hirsch, 1972).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Changes in subcutaneous fat stores are less well correlated with the development of metabolic disease than are changes in the size of visceral fat depots.
source: For example, changes in subcutaneous fat stores are less well correlated with the development of metabolic disease than are changes in the size of visceral fat depots (Merlotti et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Very low levels of leptin, too low to cause weight loss, can still correct hyperglycemia and insulin resistance in ob/ob mice.
source: This is also in agreement with another study showing that very low levels of leptin, too low to cause weight loss, can still correct hyperglycemia and insulin resistance in ob/ob mice (Hedbacker et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Lean Type two diabetics have an oligogenic form of lipodystrophy.
source: Recent studies have suggested that lean Type two diabetics have an oligogenic form of lipodystrophy and these data further suggest that relatively decreased leptin levels in this cohort may be an important component of their phenotype, a possibility that has not been formally tested (Lotta et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Relatively decreased leptin levels in lean Type two diabetics may be an important component of their phenotype.
source: Recent studies have suggested that lean Type two diabetics have an oligogenic form of lipodystrophy and these data further suggest that relatively decreased leptin levels in this cohort may be an important component of their phenotype, a possibility that has not been formally tested (Lotta et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the current findings and prior research.

claim: A small increase in fat mass from wild-type but not ob/ob mice is capable of suppressing the lipodystrophic phenotype.
source: These findings are consistent with previous studies showing that a small increase in fat mass from wild-type but not ob/ob mice is capable of suppressing the lipodystrophic phenotype (Rodeheffer et al., 2008; Gavrilova et al., 2000; Colombo et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.
